sections.title: 1. Self-reflection: be honest about where you need to grow
3. Make achievable goals: a large goal, then action steps

blocks.p: You want to make changes in your life, maybe professionally or in your emotional regulation, but you're concerned about other people, and that stops you from taking steps toward what you truly want. Here's a four-step process for making change, and hopefully some help letting go of needing permission from other people.

Personal growth is an ongoing process of improving yourself. It's not a one-time thing. Typically, it results in more feelings of pride, confidence, and satisfaction. It can also lead to more connection with other people and with yourself, and more energy to meet your life's goals.

Personal growth requires a willingness to challenge yourself, to step outside your comfort zone, and to commit to continuously learning and improving. It means looking at change as small steps, maybe small habits you pick up that snowball into other things. I think personal growth is about becoming the best version of yourself and having a fulfilling life.

That's completely up to you. I don't know what the best version of you looks like, or what a fulfilling life is to you. I know what it means to me, and I think I'm still learning that as I age. It's something you'll have to be honest with yourself about, and curious about, as time goes on.

I think these are always evolving. They're not static. As you get older and your priorities change, a fulfilling life is going to look different. The best version of myself when I was 21 is nowhere near what it is for me now. Now it has a lot to do with being a dad, being a husband, and being successful in my career. Pretty boring, I know. But the best version of myself is really about other people. How do I serve my family, the people in my career, and you as well? Yes, I'm taking care of myself, but where I'm at in life, it's more about how I can serve other people and impact the world in a positive way. Was it like that when I was 21? No. 16? No.
Personal growth is more than external success. You could work on something and change your behavior, and that's fantastic. You could make concrete marketing goals for your business and achieve them.

But in order to achieve that external success, you'll probably find there's some internal goal you need to work on, like believing in yourself more or saying kinder things to yourself. And when you do achieve that external goal, you'll probably notice it has an impact on you internally. You'll have an emotional experience of meeting it. You'll feel accomplished, proud, maybe even more determined.
So personal growth does involve observable external behaviors, but inner change either happens before it, comes along with it, or both. I think typically it's both.
Not only are you allowed to grow personally, it's necessary. As you change your life and access more positivity through your personal growth, you can also access more of your body's safety state.

The safety state is basically your body's natural biological capacity to feel safe. There are specific pathways, ventral vagal pathways, and when they're activated, you're healthier, you have more growth, and your body's able to heal itself. Dr. Porges, the creator of the theory, says it's needed for health, growth, and restoration.

So personal growth, as I understand it, directly connects to your safety state. As you grow and become more proud of yourself, as you meet your life goals and have more connection with yourself and with others, you'll have more access to safety. And as you do, your defensive states, flight, fight, shutdown, and freeze, are probably going to reduce as well.

Of course, as you set new goals to achieve, that might activate some defensive states too. But as long as you can tolerate it and ground yourself in your safety state, you'll be able to meet these goals, grow from them, and have even more distress tolerance, even more of an anchor in your safety state.
So I think you should challenge yourself, and I think it's very necessary for your general health: your physical health, and your mental health too.

You're allowed to make positive changes in your life. You don't need permission from other people. You don't need permission from me. But maybe hearing it out loud does something for you, so I'll just say it: you're allowed to grow personally, in whatever way that looks like for you.

It might be nice to have approval. It might be nice to have support. But it's also unnecessary. You are in control of your own life to some extent. There are things you do have control over, or what seems like control at least, and you do have what looks like the power to make choices that will benefit you, to stop doing some things and start doing others.

Starting a new hobby, you can choose to do that. Improving your health, you can choose to do that. Working on your relationships: these are all choices you can make, or goals you can work toward at least. No, it's not easy. Yes, it's a long process. But nobody's going to do it for you, and nobody has the power to give you permission to begin. That's up to you entirely.

You don't have to wait for somebody else to tell you it's okay to make a change. It is always possible to start. I don't care how old you are. I'm 42, and I'm still creating new goals for myself to work on, professionally, in my family, personally, and interpersonally.

If you think you do need somebody else's permission, go back to step one below and be honest with yourself. Admit it. That's one thing you can start to work on, learn more about, and maybe make a goal around.
Responsibility is a big part of this: taking personal responsibility for your own growth and your own wellbeing.

Of course it's okay to rely on each other. Right now I'm giving, and you're receiving, my thoughts and hopefully my encouragement and compassion. So it's completely okay to accept things from other people. I hope you have people in your life you can rely on: a therapist, a best friend, a spouse. I'd say mutually rely on other people. We don't want it to be a one-way street. It's okay to allow other people to support you if they're offering it. Don't demand it. It's okay to ask for help when you need it. But ultimately, you need to take responsibility for your own growth and your own wellbeing.

So instead of seeking validation from others and getting permission, focus on you. Focus on what you're not happy with in your life, what you have control over, and what you can realistically set a goal for and start making changes in, even small changes. What can you be proactive about?

Now, are there people to blame for certain aspects of your life? Undoubtedly. Are your parents on some level to blame for your current stuck polyvagal defensive state? Probably. Your family, your society, religious institutions, cultural beliefs and norms: we could blame these things up and down, and that might be completely valid. That might be completely true.

But regardless, you are still responsible for making change for yourself. You just are. The current context of your life, your current polyvagal state, the level of hope you have, that probably is a reflection of your past. Well, it is. We can make sense of why you are the way you are, why you think the way you think, why you feel the way you feel, and I won't disagree with you about that.

But this moment, the next moment, tomorrow, next month: that is up to you. That's not up to those people anymore. So I'd encourage you to embrace that, and take complete responsibility for this moment and for what happens in the future that you do have control over. Stuff's still going to pop up. Random things will happen. There will still be things working against you, and obstacles. That's life.

Both of these can be true at the same time. You can blame everybody in your past for how you are, and that might be true and valid. It's also true that you are responsible for making a change in your life. It's your life, not theirs. You make your own choices, and that can start right now.

If you're still here with me after accepting all that, the next step is to set clear goals for your personal development. That might sound like a big task, and it kind of is. I'm asking you to make change, and to take responsibility for it. I'm also telling you that you don't need anyone else's permission. This way of talking might be different for you, and you might have some pushback against it. So the solution is clear goals and clear action steps, things that are practical and doable. Setting goals and achieving them is at the core of personal growth, in my opinion.

blocks.h3: 1. Self-reflection: be honest about where you need to grow

blocks.p: Identify what's causing you distress that you have some level of control over. Maybe it's reducing the amount of junk food you eat. Maybe it's something emotional, like anger. You can't directly control the anger, but what do you have control over, or influence over, that could reduce it? It could be a behavioral goal, a career goal, or an emotional goal.
Be honest, and be compassionate with yourself. You don't have to do this with judgment. Just admit, "This is what I need to work on." Say it out loud if you need to. Write it down.

Learn about what you identified in step one. If you need to reduce your anger, learn what anger is, where it comes from, and how other people have reduced theirs. Instead of looking at anger as a bad thing, can you look at whether there's a more positive side to it? Do a deep dive.

Learning can be normalizing. Hopefully you won't feel like there's something wrong with you, and you'll notice that other people have anger too, or are having a hard time in their business just like you are, or in their relationship just like you are. So learning can give you normalization and validation. It also gives you ideas to work with, so you're not on an island by yourself with the problem you want to change.

That could mean learning more about your polyvagal state: how you got stuck, and how you're staying stuck. The Polyvagal Institute is a good resource. Dr. Porges's writings are difficult, but largely accessible, I think. If you're into this stuff, you could probably handle it. Or learn about attachment. Or if you're into internal family systems or shadow work or ego stuff, I don't like it, but all right, have at it. Just learn.

blocks.h3: 3. Make achievable goals: a large goal, then action steps

blocks.p: Identify the large goal: "This is what I want my life to look like."

Focus on what you do want, not what you don't want. Instead of "I want to reduce my anger," which is fine, ask what you want in its place. More calm? Then the goal becomes, "I want to increase how much calm I'm feeling." You could even give it a number: right now I'm feeling calm zero times per day, and I want to increase that to once per day. Or maybe it's improving your relationship satisfaction, or communication with your spouse. That's the bigger goal.

Keep that, and then break it into action steps: things you can do that are measurable and achievable, to reach the larger goal. This will help you stay on track, help you measure effectiveness, and give you something to work on every day. Instead of just saying, "I wish my life was different," every day you can say, "Oh, I'm supposed to do this action step."

Say your goal is, "I want to live with more calm and stillness in my life." The action step could be, "I will start each morning with no electronics for one hour, for one week." Be very specific about what you want to do, and maybe even more specific about when it takes place each day. Hopefully it leads to the goal of living with a bit more calm every day.

But it might not. Maybe that action step is too much for you, or just not effective for what you want to accomplish. That's why taking smaller, mindful steps toward personal growth is so important, and that connects to step four.

Personal growth is not a one-time thing. You don't do it in one day. It requires consistent effort and dedication, so small and mindful steps are key. Attempt the action step, and then adjust it as you need to.
Doing it mindfully means that as you try the action step, you ask yourself how you feel about it. Say you go with no electronics for one hour in the morning. Some questions to ask:

ul: In super simple terms: does this feel more good or more bad? Do I like it or dislike it?
A little more complex: does it feel more calm or less calm? When I sit in silence for one hour every morning, do I feel more or less calm?
Is another emotion coming up for me, and is it tolerable?
Does sitting in silence for an hour every morning help me breathe easier and think more clearly?

blocks.p: If so, you're probably starting to make steps toward your larger goal of feeling more calm, in place of feeling anger.

If you find the action step is ineffective, "This is more bad than good, more dislike than like, and I don't feel calm when I do this," then come up with something different. The goal can stay, "I want to live with more calm and stillness in my life." But the revised action step could be, "I will start each morning with no electronics for thirty minutes." Maybe an hour was too much. Or revised action step B could be, "I will walk for ten minutes every day before lunch." Maybe movement is a better idea for you, and ten minutes of mindful walking might bring you closer to calm than silence in the morning.
Irene Lyon described this kind of trial and error well when she was on the podcast:

q: What can I do that will help my physiology come down? And that is trial and error and that's being experimental and curious.

blocks.p: These little steps should be approachable and tolerable, but they should be challenging. You might have to step outside your comfort zone a little, so do it in ways that are challenging but manageable. Then, as you master it, make it a little more difficult. If the hour each morning is going great, you might extend it thirty minutes, or keep it the way it is and add the walk before lunch every day.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: It's important to have people in your life who are supportive and positive. There's a good chance you don't have that. I think people who live in a very traumatized state, day in and day out, have a harder time identifying safe people in their life. But we all need them. We're humans. We need each other. We are a social species.

You want to surround yourself with people who are positive and supportive, ideally people who are in their own safety state, or have enough access to it, because they'll be able to provide you with something called co-regulation. It's a biological process, and it's unconscious.

When a mammal has access to its safety state, it gives cues of safety to others. Dogs are probably the easiest example. A dog will get close to you, want to be pet, look you in the eyes, wag its tail. Touch, eye contact, playing, running around: these are the safety cues a dog uses when it's in a safety state. It'll want to get closer to you and play with you. It's biologically compelled to.

Now imagine that basic idea with the people in your life. I'm not saying other people want to be pet by you. I'm saying people in their safety state will hopefully gravitate toward you, give you smiles and eye crinkles, be compassionate, and listen to you. They'll also challenge you and encourage you, ideally. People who can offer co-regulation, support, and challenge: that's ideally what we want.

It's not easy to find. It really isn't. You could check your local area for clubs or groups that meet up and might be a good fit for you. Maybe you don't have a core group of people. Maybe you have one person. That's fantastic. That's someone.

Maybe there are other people in your life you need to cut out entirely, or spend less time with. Don't be afraid to distance yourself. Actually, let me rephrase that: it's okay to be afraid to distance yourself from those people. Creating healthier boundaries is difficult. But it can be helpful.

As you prioritize your goals and your self-development, and spend more time with the people who provide you safety cues and co-regulation, you'll have less time for people who are more toxic or negative, or just neutral. Maybe there's something to develop there, or maybe they're fine just as work or classroom acquaintances.

The other option, which is more realistic, less than ideal, but still a very good option, is to find people online. In person is best, because of the face-to-face contact. But it's a lot easier to find people online: Facebook groups, private communities, forums or discussion boards with people who have similar interests.

Try them out. Join, and see how it is. You have to vet them. If it feels toxic, not a good fit, or too negative, you can leave. You don't have to be a part of it anymore. I think it's a lot easier to leave those spaces than in-person ones with relationships you've established, even if they're not the best relationships. So online gives you a chance to try things out, and then back out, or invest more of your time and energy if it's worth it.
